Pay
pā
v.t. (rendering Hebrew shalam, Greek apodidōmi)
From French payer, Latin pacare, to appease or satisfy, from pax, peace — to pay is to make peace with a claim. Hebrew shalam carries the same idea and the same root as shalom: to make whole, to complete, to render what restores the balance.

Biblical Definition

Payment in Scripture is the completion of an obligation, and the Bible is severe about obligations that are contracted lightly. Vows come first: “When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed” (Ecclesiastes 5:4), and the Psalmist joins payment to worship itself — “Offer unto God thanksgiving; and pay thy vows unto the most High” (Psalm 50:14). Civil obligation is treated with the same seriousness: “For this cause pay ye tribute also: for they are God's ministers, attending continually upon this very thing” (Romans 13:6) — taxes are paid to men who are, whether they know it or not, ministers of God. And the parable of the unmerciful servant sets the whole matter in the light of the gospel: the lord “commanded him to be sold, and his wife, and children, and all that he had, and payment to be made” (Matthew 18:25) — a debt of ten thousand talents, entirely beyond payment, forgiven outright, after which the forgiven man took his fellowservant by the throat over a hundred pence. The doctrine is plain: God requires that men pay what they owe; and He knows that the debt every man owes Him could never be paid, which is why the gospel is not an easier payment plan but a cancelled account and a new heart to match.

Webster 1828 Definition

To discharge a debt; to render what is due; to satisfy a claim. In Scripture, the command to pay what is vowed and not defer it, to pay vows unto the most High, to pay tribute to the civil ruler as God's minister, and the debtor commanded to be sold that payment might be made.

expand to see more

PAY, v.t. 1. To discharge a debt; to deliver to a creditor the value of a debt, in money or in goods.

2. To compensate; to requite; to make amends for; as, to pay a man for his labour.

3. To render what is due to a superior; as, to pay homage, to pay tribute, to pay vows.

4. From French payer, Latin pacare, to appease or satisfy, from pax, peace.

5. In Scripture, pay that which thou hast vowed, Eccl. 5; for this cause pay ye tribute also, Rom. 13.

Key Scripture

Ecclesiastes 5:4 — "When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed."

Psalm 50:14 — "Offer unto God thanksgiving; and pay thy vows unto the most High:"

Romans 13:6 — "For for this cause pay ye tribute also: for they are God's ministers, attending continually upon this very thing."

Matthew 18:25 — "But forasmuch as he had not to pay, his lord commanded him to be sold, and his wife, and children, and all that he had, and payment to be made."

Modern Corruption

Vows and obligations are treated as expressions of present feeling rather than binding commitments, so that a man may walk away from what he swore; and the forgiveness of an unpayable debt is received without the mercy toward others it was meant to produce.

expand to see more

Ecclesiastes 5 warns against the mouth that is rash before God, and the culture has industrialised rashness. Vows — marital, membership, ordination, financial — are increasingly understood as statements of current intention that lapse when the feeling changes, and the language of authenticity is used to dignify the retreat: to keep a vow one no longer feels would be dishonest. Scripture takes the contrary view throughout. Psalm 15 marks out the man who sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not, as one who shall abide in God's tabernacle. It is precisely when a vow costs what was not anticipated that keeping it becomes worship. The Preacher's counsel is not that vows are unwise but that they are serious: better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.

The unmerciful servant sets the second corruption before us in a form nobody can miss. He was forgiven ten thousand talents — an absurd, unpayable sum, chosen precisely because no servant could ever have owed or repaid it — and then throttled a fellowservant over a hundred pence. The parable is the Lord's exposition of the petition He had just taught: forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. It does not teach that a man earns pardon by forgiving; it teaches that a man who has really received pardon of that size cannot hold a hundred pence against his brother, and that where he does, his profession is exposed. The principle to recover joins both halves of the entry: pay what you owe to men, and remember what has been cancelled for you by God.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shalam, to make whole, complete, or repay, from the same root as shalom; nathan, to give; Greek apodidōmi, to give back or render, and tinō, to pay a penalty.

expand to see more

Hebrew shalam (H7999) — to be complete, to make good, to repay; the root of shalom, peace as wholeness restored.

Hebrew neder (H5088) — a vow; the voluntary obligation Ecclesiastes 5 commands men to pay without delay.

Greek apodidōmi (G591) — to give back, render, repay; “render therefore to all their dues” (Romans 13:7).

Greek opheilē (G3782) — a debt, that which is owed; the word behind “forgive us our debts.”

Greek talanton (G5007) — a talent, a very large weight of silver; ten thousand of them is the unpayable debt of Matthew 18:24.

Usage

"Of vows kept without delay: pay that which thou hast vowed (Ecclesiastes 5:4)."

"Of civil obligation as a duty to God: For this cause pay ye tribute also: for they are God's ministers (Romans 13:6)."

"Of a debt beyond all payment: commanded him to be sold... and payment to be made (Matthew 18:25)."
